title: Knowledge Check 7: Lessons 31-34
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 31-34 of the ai-adoption series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A manager builds the AI tool inventory from procurement records only. Based on Lesson 31, what will that inventory miss?
options: Nothing important, because procurement records capture every paid tool by definition

Tools bought through product-led growth on team cards and expense reports, and AI tiers that arrived inside existing software renewals, so the inventory must pull twelve months of charges plus expense reports and compare department head lists against them
Only free trials, which do not matter because they cost nothing
Only the tools that failed a security review, since those are removed from procurement records
questions.explanation: Lesson 31 states that a large share of AI buying never passes through procurement (Menlo's product-led growth and shadow AI figures), and that AI often arrives inside software the company already owns as an upgraded tier, which raises cost without adding a visible line item. It prescribes pulling twelve months of charges including team cards and expense reports, adding embedded tiers and free tools that became habit, then comparing department head lists to the statements, because the gap between the two is the real inventory.

questions.question: Why does Lesson 31 insist that consolidation happen at renewal dates rather than as soon as the decision is made?
options: Because vendors legally cannot be contacted outside a renewal window

Because a forced mid-contract cutover pays twice for the same job and teaches the organization that consolidation is painful, while a renewal date is when ending a contract is cheap and a new one is negotiable
Because employees need at least a year to learn any new tool before switching
Because the lesson recommends waiting until the annual audit to make any decisions
questions.explanation: Lesson 31 describes consolidation as having a natural rhythm: contracts end on dates, and attempting a forced cutover mid-contract means paying twice for the same job, once to the old vendor and once to the new one, which teaches the organization that consolidation is painful. It therefore builds a renewal calendar from the inventory, names a migration owner, archives what must be kept, requests data deletion in writing, and ends the contract before auto-renewal rather than after.

questions.question: A team asks to add a second design tool to the stack because it generates better images for their specific work. Under Lesson 31's front-door controls, what has to be true for that request to proceed?
options: The tool must be free, since free tools do not count against the stack
The team must wait for the annual audit before any new tool can be considered
Another tool leaves the stack, or the requester shows the new tool does a job the primary cannot, with a named owner and a review date recorded as an exception
The department head must approve it, and approval alone is sufficient to add it
questions.explanation: Lesson 31 sets out a one-in, one-out rule for new tools in an existing category: a tool enters only when another leaves or the requester shows it does a job the primary cannot. Exceptions are allowed, but the four-sentence test requires naming the specific job, the team, the capability the primary lacks, and a review date. Free tools are not exempt, and departmental approval alone is drift rather than a decision with an expiry.

questions.question: A finance director approves seats for every employee who is technically eligible, on an annual commitment, so that nobody is blocked on day one. Based on Lesson 32, what has that decision removed?
options: Nothing important, because full coverage is the end state any rollout is aiming for
The waitlist, which is a measurement of declared intent, and the ability to shrink the count mid-term, since adding seats later is a phone call while removing them is a negotiation
The need to provision accounts through the identity provider, because bulk assignment replaces group-based provisioning
The requirement to measure adoption, because a fully licensed population is the same as a fully adopted one
questions.explanation: Lesson 32 separates eligibility from adoption and argues you should almost never buy to the eligible population at the start. Buying to eligibility converts a behavior question into a sunk cost and removes the waitlist, which tells you which teams are pulling. It also conflicts with the contract asymmetry the lesson calls the single most important fact: adding seats mid-term is usually easy, removing them is not, so the purchased count holds until renewal.

questions.question: An organization builds its entitlement groups as a department group containing team groups, assigns the license to the department group, and finds that part of the department never received access. What does Lesson 32 identify as the cause and the fix?
options: The license count was too low for the group, so the fix is to buy more seats than the group contains
SCIM had not been enabled, so the fix is to turn on directory sync and wait for propagation
When a license is applied to a nested group only the immediate first-level user members receive it, so entitlement groups should be kept flat and the nesting left to the directory elsewhere
Direct assignments had already been made to those users, so the fix is to clear every direct assignment in the tenant
questions.explanation: Lesson 32 lists nested groups as the first of four provisioning edges, citing the documented behavior that applying a license to a nested group licenses only immediate first-level user members. The recommended fix is flat entitlement groups, one per job category, with nesting handled elsewhere. The other options misidentify the mechanism: group licensing already requires a license for each unique member, SCIM is not the cause of the nesting limit, and direct assignments are a separate edge.

questions.question: At day 120 a program reports 1,000 assigned seats and 720 users active in the last 30 days, and the steering group calls that 72 percent adoption. What does Lesson 32 say is wrong with that number?
options: Nothing, because active in 30 days is the standard definition of adoption
It is too pessimistic, because assigned seats always undercount real access once shared accounts are included
It mixes layers and windows: the funnel separates purchased, assigned, technically enabled, active and habitual, and the habitual count is what predicts whether the renewal is defensible
It is irrelevant because adoption should only be measured once per year at renewal
questions.explanation: Lesson 32 argues one number cannot describe a rollout because each gap between layers has a different cause and owner. The funnel counts purchased, assigned, technically enabled, active in a stated window, weekly active and habitual, and the lesson notes that whoever sets the activity window decides the adoption figure. The worked example shows the same cohort at 1,000 assigned, 940 enabled, 720 active in 30 days, 410 weekly and 330 habitual.

questions.question: A program's habitual use rate has held between 38 and 41 percent for three quarters. Fanned out, cohort curves show the February group reached 54 percent and flattened, May reached 47, and the August cohort reached 39 percent and was still climbing at quarter end. Based on Lesson 33, what does that pattern indicate?
options: Saturation, because the aggregate has stopped rising, so the program should stop buying seats and shift to depth
A stall, because later cohorts are performing worse than earlier ones, so the enablement program should be rebuilt from scratch
A measurement defect, because cohort curves cannot differ from the aggregate if the same definition is used

Later cohorts improving while starting lower, which points to an enablement and workflow-fit problem rather than saturation, since a saturation plateau would show curves converging on a similar asymptote
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 distinguishes three causes of a flat aggregate. Converging curves that reach a similar asymptote indicate saturation. Curves that start at the same height and descend faster in later waves indicate enablement debt. Curves that flatten lower than earlier ones but are still climbing indicate exactly what the August cohort shows: later cohorts have harder jobs or worse onboarding, which is a scoping and enablement fact. The worked example traces the gap to a kickoff cut from 90 minutes to 20, and answers with a rebuilt day-one session rather than more licenses.

questions.question: In Q4 an organization sees habitual use rate fall from 41 to 38 percent, returning rate fall from 72 to 64 percent, and depth fall from 6.0 to 5.2 actions per active user. What does Lesson 33 say the order of investigation should be?
options: Start with a strategy review of the AI roadmap, since three metrics moving together is a program failure signal

Start with the cheap and common explanations in order: composition of the base, window and delay, instrument and definition changes, calendar effects, then run chart and control chart rules, stopping at the first check that explains the movement
Start with control chart limits, because statistical rules must confirm the decline before any business explanation is considered
Start with a user survey, because only users can explain why usage changed
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 gives a fixed six-check sequence in that order because the cheap explanations are also the most common, and a program that opens with a strategy debate about a data defect wastes a quarter of goodwill. The worked example runs the same sequence: a reorganisation moved 60 people out of the reachable population, December holiday weeks repeated a known seasonal dip, and two metrics had been redefined or were being read from a dashboard with a different window. Two of the four metrics in that example were instrument problems, which is why arithmetic gets ruled out before behavior.

questions.question: An operator plots weekly active users on a run chart with the median as the centre line and sees seven consecutive weekly points below the median, with no single point far outside the pattern. Based on Lesson 33, how should that be read?
options: As noise, because no point broke the three sigma limit and only extreme points count
As a shift, because six or more consecutive points on one side of the median is the run chart rule for a shift, which means the movement deserves investigation even without an extreme point
As proof that the program declined, because any run of points below the median is a confirmed decline
As a trend, because a trend is defined as five or more consecutive points moving in one direction
questions.explanation: Lesson 33 cites the run chart rules: a shift is six or more consecutive points above or below the median, a trend is five or more consecutive points all increasing or decreasing, and an astronomical point is one so far outside the pattern that it needs a specific explanation. Seven points below the median therefore meets the shift rule, which is a signal to look rather than a conclusion. The lesson also pairs that with its decision rule: a single quarter with a movement gets a note, and two consecutive quarters with a sustained shift plus a nameable mechanism gets a decision.

questions.question: A team connects an assistant to the CRM using a single shared service credential so the pilot can start quickly. During testing, a manager with restricted CRM access asks the assistant to summarize an account she cannot open, and it does. Based on Lesson 34, what is the correct response?
options: Keep the connection and add a line to the AI policy telling users not to ask about accounts they cannot access
Rebuild the connection on mirrored user permissions and adopt a standing acceptance test: three questions it must answer correctly for a named restricted user, and one it must refuse
Cancel the CRM connection permanently, because rung three integration is too risky for any organization
Leave the connection as is but move the use case back to rung one manual copy and paste for that user
questions.explanation: Lesson 34's worked example describes exactly this finding: the connector used a shared service credential that read the whole CRM, so nothing had leaked yet but everything would have. The fix is to rebuild on mirrored permissions, where the AI can only reach what the asking user could already open, and to make the acceptance test permanent, including one question the connection must refuse. The lesson states plainly that a connection that cannot refuse is not ready, and that policy text is not a substitute for permission design.

questions.question: An organization has budget for three integration projects this quarter and a long list of candidates, including a read-only connection to curated policy documents, a write connection that would let AI send rate quotes to customers, and a read connection to live shipment status. How does Lesson 34 say to order the work?
options: Start with the project that has the largest announced business value, then the next largest, regardless of what the connection can change
Start with the write connection, because it removes the most manual work and therefore proves value fastest

Order by reversibility of the worst likely failure first, so read-only connections to curated content go first and write connections to anything leaving the company go last, then weigh the size of the named population and whether the connection removes a step rather than adding one
Order alphabetically by system name so that all departments are treated equally and nothing looks political
questions.explanation: Lesson 34 gives an explicit ranking order: reversibility of the worst likely failure first, then the size of the named population that benefits, then whether the connection removes a step rather than adding a new destination. It states that read-only connections to curated content almost always go first and write connections to anything that leaves the company go last without exception, and the worked example refuses the quoting use case until the read tier has three months of clean answers behind it.

questions.question: Six months after a successful connection to the document store goes live, usage quietly declines. The connection is still up, the sync still runs, and nobody has filed a ticket. Based on Lesson 34, what is the most likely cause and the right control?
options: The model got worse, so the fix is to switch to a newer model and re-run the pilot

The index went stale and the assistant kept answering confidently from old content, so the fix is a freshness expectation per corpus, a visible last-updated stamp, and a weekly canary question owned by a named person, because you watch the answers rather than the uptime
The users need more training on prompting, so the fix is a second round of the original onboarding session
The licence must have expired, so the fix is to check the invoice and renew the connector add-on
questions.explanation: Lesson 34 describes stale index failure as a connection that works, syncs, and serves content that stopped being curated, with the assistant answering confidently from old material while nobody notices. It prescribes a freshness expectation per corpus and a visible last-updated stamp, and names silent breakage as the failure where nobody files a ticket because nobody knows the answers stopped being current. The stated rule is to watch the answers, not the uptime, with a canary question checked weekly by a named person.
